source:
Alma: Downtown foot traffic is down thirty percent and both anchor stores are gone. The cause is simple: the commuter base never came back after remote work normalized.
Ben: The commuters come back Thursday to Saturday. What killed weekday traffic is that parking tripled to thirty dollars.
Alma: Garage revenue data shows occupancy fell even when prices were unchanged early in the pandemic.
Ben: And yet the districts that kept cheap parking recovered twice as fast with the same remote-work rates.
Alma: Those districts also had less visible disorder, which confounds your comparison.
Ben: Which is why I say pricing, not safety, is the lever we control.

extraction.mainQuestion: What is primarily causing the decline in downtown foot traffic?

positions.label: Remote work emptied downtown
positions.thesis: The foot-traffic decline is caused primarily by the loss of the daily commuter base after remote work normalized.
positions.steelman: Occupancy fell before parking prices moved, which points to the vanished commuter base rather than later price changes.

groundingQuotes.quote: The cause is simple: the commuter base never came back after remote work normalized.

positions.label: Parking prices killed weekday traffic
positions.thesis: Weekday traffic declined mainly because parking tripled in price, not because commuters disappeared.
positions.steelman: Districts with identical remote-work rates but cheaper parking recovered faster, which isolates pricing as the controllable cause.

groundingQuotes.quote: What killed weekday traffic is that parking tripled to thirty dollars.

claims.statement: The decline in downtown foot traffic is caused primarily by the loss of the daily commuter base.

resolution.condition: Compare weekday visitor origins and volumes before and after remote-work normalization, controlling for parking prices.

groundingQuotes.quote: Garage revenue data shows occupancy fell even when prices were unchanged early in the pandemic.

claims.statement: The weekday traffic decline is driven mainly by parking prices tripling to thirty dollars.

resolution.condition: A district-level comparison of recovery rates at differing price points with matched remote-work exposure.

groundingQuotes.quote: the districts that kept cheap parking recovered twice as fast with the same remote-work rates.

claims.statement: Districts with cheaper parking also differ in visible disorder, so their faster recovery does not isolate pricing as the cause.

resolution.condition: A comparison controlling for disorder measures as well as parking prices.

groundingQuotes.quote: Those districts also had less visible disorder, which confounds your comparison.

commonGroundCandidates.statement: Downtown foot traffic is down about thirty percent and both anchor stores have closed.

groundingQuotes.quote: Downtown foot traffic is down thirty percent and both anchor stores are gone.

commonGroundCandidates.statement: Commuters still return late in the week.

groundingQuotes.quote: The commuters come back Thursday to Saturday.

disagreementCandidates.question: What is the primary cause of the downtown foot-traffic decline?
disagreementCandidates.summary: Both accept the same facts; Alma's causal model centers lost commuters, Ben's centers parking prices.

participantStances.stance: Tripled parking prices did the damage.

disagreementCandidates.resolutionCondition: Causal decomposition of traffic by commuter origin and price exposure.

disagreementCandidates.question: Do cross-district parking comparisons isolate pricing as a cause?
disagreementCandidates.summary: Ben treats faster recovery in cheap-parking districts as decisive; Alma says disorder confounds it.

participantStances.stance: Same remote work, different prices, different outcomes.
Those districts differ in disorder too.

caveats: This maps competing causal models over agreed facts; it does not establish which cause dominates.
